exampleAnswers.title: Identifying the Multiplicity of a Root of a Polynomial

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true with respect to the polynomial $p(x)=(x-8)^2(x+5)^4(x-4)?$

  1. The root $x=8$ of $p(x)$ is a multiple root
  2. The root $x=-5$ of $p(x)$ is a simple root
  3. The root $x=4$ of $p(x)$ is a simple root
question.explanation:
The multiplicity of a root of a polynomial equals the exponent of its corresponding factor in the factorization of the polynomial. A simple root has a multiplicity of $1,$ while a multiple root has a multiplicity that is greater than $1.$

From the factored form, we can tell that the roots of $p(x)$ are $x=8,$ $x=-5,$ and $x=4.$

  • Statement I is true. The factor $(x-8)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=8$ has multiplicity $2.$

  • Statement II is false. The factor $(x+5)$ has an exponent of $4$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-5$ has multiplicity $4.$

  • Statement III is true. The factor $(x-4)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=4$ has multiplicity $1.$

question.text: Which root(s) of the polynomial $P(x)=(x+3)(x^2-4)^3$ have multiplicity $3?$
question.explanation:
The multiplicity of a root of a polynomial equals the exponent of its corresponding factor in the factorization of the polynomial.

First, let's factor $P(x)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} P(x)&= (x+3)(x^2-4)^3\\[3pt] &= (x+3)((x+2)(x-2))^3\\[3pt] &=(x+3) (x+2)^3 (x-2)^3 \end{align*}

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

  • The factor $(x+3)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $P(x).$ So the root $x=-3$ has multiplicity $1.$

  • The factor $(x+2)$ has an exponent of $3$ in the factored form of $P(x).$ So the root $x=-2$ has multiplicity $3.$

  • The factor $(x-2)$ has an exponent of $3$ in the factored form of $P(x).$ So the root $x=2$ has multiplicity $3.$

Therefore, the roots with multiplicity $3$ are $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

question.text: What is the multiplicity of the root $x=5$ in the polynomial $p(x)=x^3-6x^2-x+30?$
question.explanation:
Since $x=5$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-5)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-5)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-5)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-5)$ using synthetic division:

$x^3$ $x^2$ $x^1$ $x^0$
$\color{red}5$ $1$ $-6$ $-1$ $30$
$\color{gray}\downarrow$ $5$ $-5$ $-30$
$1$ $-1$ $-6$ $0$

Therefore,

\[ \dfrac{p(x)}{x-5} = x^2 - x - 6, \]

which means that

\[ p(x) = (x-5) (x^2 - x - 6). \]

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

\begin{align*} p(x) &= (x-5) (x-3)(x+2). \end{align*}

The factor $(x-5)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=5$ has multiplicity $1.$

question.text: The multiplicity of the root $x=1$ in the polynomial $p(x)=x^3 + 4 x^2 - 11 x+6$ is
question.explanation:
Since $x=1$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

$x^3$ $x^2$ $x^1$ $x^0$
$\color{red}1$ $1$ $4$ $-11$ $6$
$\color{gray}\downarrow$ $1$ $5$ $-6$
$1$ $5$ $-6$ $0$

Therefore,

\[ \dfrac{p(x)}{x-1} = x^2 + 5x -6, \]

which means that

\[ p(x) = (x-1) (x^2 + 5x - 6). \]

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

\begin{align*} p(x) &= (x-1) (x-1)(x+6)\\[3pt] & = (x+6) (x-1)^2. \end{align*}

The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2}.$

question.text: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x) = 16x^3-4x^2$ have multiplicity $1?$
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial.

For this polynomial, we can factor by noting that the greatest common factor of $16x^3$ and $-4x^2$ is $4x^2{:}$

\begin{align*} p(x) &= 16x^3-4x^2\\[3pt] &= 4x^2(4x-1) \end{align*}

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

  • The factor $x^2$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

  • The factor $(4x-1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=\dfrac 14$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=\dfrac 14$ has multiplicity $1.$

question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial.

For this polynomial, we can factor by noting that the greatest common factor of $8x^3$ and $6x^2$ is $2x^2{:}$

\begin{align*} p(x) &=8x^3 + 6x^2\\[3pt] &= 2x^2(4x+3) \end{align*}

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

  • The factor $x$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

  • The factor $(4x+3)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-\dfrac{3}{4}$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}$ has multiplicity $2.$

question.text: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x) = 2x^3 + x^2 + 32x + 16$ have multiplicity $2?$
question.explanation:
We factor the cubic by grouping, and simplify until the polynomial is fully factored:

\begin{align*} p(x) &= 2x^3 + x^2 + 32x + 16 \\[5pt] &= x^2(2x+1) + 16(2x+1) \\[5pt] &= (x^2+16)(2x+1) \end{align*}

Note that the factor $(x^2+16)$ cannot be factored any further, and it does not have any real roots.

The only real root of $p(x)$ comes from the factor $(2x+1).$ This factor has a root of $x=-\dfrac{1}{2},$ and the exponent of the factor is $1.$ Therefore, the root $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, there is no root with multiplicity $2.$

question.text: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x) = 9 x^3 + 9 x^2 - x - 1$ have multiplicity $1?$
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. For this polynomial, we can factor by grouping:

\begin{align*} p(x) &= 9 x^3 + 9 x^2 - x - 1\\[5pt] &= 9x^2(x+1) - 1(x+1) \\[5pt] &= (9x^2-1)(x+1) \\[5pt] &= (3x+1)(3x-1)(x+1) \end{align*}

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

  • The factor $(3x+1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-\dfrac 13$ has multiplicity $1.$

  • The factor $(3x-1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=\dfrac 13$ has multiplicity $1.$

  • The factor $(x+1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-1$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, the roots $x=-1, \, -\dfrac 13, \, \dfrac 13$ all have multiplicity $1.$
